records.sourceFile: Sport-related Concussion Can be Prevented by Injury Prevention Program.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of eight prospective controlled studies (2,571 participants; 1,281 intervention, 1,290 control), with searches to March 2024. The pooled incidence rate ratio for sport-related concussion was 0.66 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.85, p = .002), which the authors report as a 34% lower incidence in intervention groups, with no heterogeneity (I2 = 0). Neither intervention type (physical training IRR 0.61; educational IRR 0.76, non-significant) nor exposure context (match IRR 0.67; practice IRR 0.71) significantly moderated the effect.
records.limitations: The pooled estimate rests on eight mostly non-randomized studies (three cluster RCTs; mean NIH quality score 7, rated fair), in three sports, with mostly male samples. The educational subgroup is two American Football Heads Up Football studies, so the non-significant moderator tests do not show equal efficacy across program types or contexts.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the 34% reduction as proven for all sports, both sexes and any program type, when the evidence is mainly male rugby, soccer and American football samples.

changes: limitations: added the text-versus-table conflict: Discussion says physical training IRR 0.61 'was not statistically significant', but Table 5 CI 0.42 to 0.89 excludes 1.
findings: added data-point counts for subgroups (Table 5 k = 8 physical, k = 3 educational).
verification.residualConcerns: Physical training subgroup: Table 5 CI (0.42 to 0.89) excludes 1, yet the Discussion says the reduction was not significant. Female Athletes tag rests on one mixed-sex study (Peek 2023); 7 of 8 studies were male only.
